newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Norman Mailer finds Jesus, sort of.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Norman Mailer finds Jesus, sort of.

text.p: Next year the U.S. literary establishment will no doubt celebrate Norman Mailer's 75th birthday and the 50th anniversary of the publication of his most famous novel, "The Naked and the Dead."

Right now people are busy beating up the grand old man of American letters for his latest book, which the critics charge is an act of chutzpah -- the Yiddish word for unmitigated gall and a term often applied to Mailer.

That is because the book is called "The Gospel According to the Son" and is an account of the life of Jesus as told by Jesus. As he explains in the opening passages, "For those who would ask how my words came to this page, I would tell them to look upon it as a small miracle. (My gospel, after all, will speak of miracles.)"

Small miracles not withstanding, Mailer is getting toasted, roasted, hammered and, in some reviews, crucified. Some critics say he has made Jesus bland and New-Agey, others complain he has made him into yet another 20th Century celebrity, while still others think the book is just too faithful to the Gospels to be of interest or that Mailer's Jesus is just too "full of bumper-sticker aphorisms and mixed metaphors," as the New York Observer critic wrote.
STICKING TO SEX, DEATH AND MARILYN MONROE

Also they are not used to Mailer writing about a religious figure and would feel more comfortable if he stuck to his usual subjects: sex, death, Marilyn Monroe, John F. Kennedy, the CIA or Lee Harvey Oswald.

The small beauties of language in the book and some of its daring theological constructs -- like its questioning of God's omnipotence or its portrait of a worried Christ to whom God no longer talks -- have gone unnoticed in the Mailer-bashing.

"Sometimes Mr Mailer's Jesus sounds an awful lot like a guest on Oprah. Sometimes he sounds like Do and Ti (aka Bo and Peep, Pig and Guinea). And sometimes he sounds like Luke Skywalker, the apprentice Jedi trying to master the Force," New York Times book critic Michiko Kakutani wrote in a review that especially irritated Mailer.
He says he does not mind the criticism per se but he does mind that the review came out two weeks before publication, early enough to set the tone for those that followed.
"Michiko Kakutani is a confirmed pervert on the subject of Narman Mailer and this time she did it early. I am amazed that the Times does this," Mailer told Reuters recently.

He admitted that, yes, he did expect criticism for doing a book about Jesus in the first person and, yes, he had visions of cartoons in which a short, pudgy Mailer is nailed to the cross and, yes, his expectations were not disappointed.

But he said he did the book because "the older I get, the more a book has to appeal to me and this one appealed to me. I read the New Testament two years ago and if you take away all the great sayings of Jesus it is not a great book. It seems well written because people grow up with it. The first three Gospels are written by committee. You can feel the compromise like an Arab-Israeli peace talk."

After joking about how hard it was to resist writing about "the Big Jew," Mailer stopped himself and said, "One of the most beautful lines in the Gospels is 'God gave his only son for us.' But it did not ring true. If God is all good then he is not all powertful. If God is all powerful then he is not all good. I am a disbeliever in the omnipotence of God because of the Holocaust. But for 35 years or so I have been believing that he is doing the best he can."

The surprise is that Mailer, an old socialist, is a believer in God, an experience he credits, perhaps jokingly, to marijuana use many decades ago. And another surprise is that he is a believer in Jesus, sort of.

"No one knows the real story. It is not recoverable. What I feel is important is not the historical reality but the psychological reality ... Novelists, when we create characters, we believe in them. (You) have to be sincere, you believe in the characters if you are writing about them.
"Do I believe in Jesus? I did when I was writing the book. ... He probably existed. It is hard to believe this (Christianity) was all built by people seeking political and religious power."
